messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mereana Tane had worked for most of her adult life as a network engineer, a role she still held part-time from a home office in Brisbane after her husband’s death. Long before she sought help, she had lived with the aftermath of an assault that occurred late one evening when she was coming back to her car after a work dinner. A man she did not know came up too close, reeking of alcohol, and when she turned away from him he grabbed her before she could reach for her keys. She remembered the shock of being held, the helplessness of not being able to stop what happened, and the way her body felt exposed and overpowered in a way that left her ashamed for months afterward. What troubled her most was not only the violence itself but the sense that, in that moment, she had acted in ways that went against who she believed herself to be; she had frozen, then complied with demands she still found humiliating to recall. Since then, Mereana had come to believe that bad things could happen to her no matter how carefully she managed herself, and that belief had become part of how she moved through the world.

At first she tried to put the event behind her, but the body-based reminders kept forcing their way in. The smell of alcohol in a lift, a colleague leaning in for a hug at a farewell, or someone speaking to her with an easy emotional closeness she had not invited could hit her with such force that she would pull back sharply, stiffen, or leave the room. She found herself avoiding intimacy in any form, not only romantic but also the warmth of friends and relatives, because affection had become tied in her mind to danger and to the shame of being caught off guard. When those reminders appeared, she responded by tightening her life around control: she restricted her eating with a severity that felt almost disciplined to her, and she gave up pleasant activities she used to enjoy, including Sunday gatherings and swimming with a neighbour, because pleasure felt indulgent and unsafe. In her mind, these habits gave her something she could govern when so much else had once been taken from her. Yet the more she withdrew, the more alone and strained she felt, and that isolation fed the same beliefs that had been forming since the assault: that she was damaged, that her body bore the mark of what happened, and that she had somehow failed herself. Those thoughts made her even more likely to pull away from affection and closeness the next time they were offered, and to retreat further into strict routines that she experienced as the only reliable protection.

Her sense of threat had become constant and practical. Everywhere she went, Mereana scanned for potential weapons or dangerous objects, whether she was in the kitchen, at the train station, or walking through the open-plan office where she occasionally supervised junior staff. She noticed knives, bottle openers, screwdrivers, even a heavy keyring in a stranger’s hand, and could not easily dismiss them. Even when people assured her she was safe, she found it impossible to believe them; the assurance never touched the part of her that expected danger to arrive quickly and without warning. She also reacted with alarm when someone touched her unexpectedly, such as a hand on her shoulder while she was bent over her laptop or a casual brush against her arm in a crowded corridor. These reactions were not separate from her coping but woven into it. Because she was constantly watching for danger, she became more determined to keep control wherever she could, and the strict eating, the refusal of enjoyment, and the avoidance of closeness all deepened. At the same time, those strategies kept her life narrow and deprived, leaving more space for fear and for the belief that her world was permanently unsafe.

Mereana eventually sought help after her daughter told her she had become impossible to reach: she no longer came to family dinners, declined hugs from the grandchildren, and grew tense at the slightest unexpected touch. The final push came after a work meeting in which a new contractor, laughing too loudly, carried the smell of alcohol from a nearby pub into the conference room; Mereana had frozen, then spent the rest of the day checking exits and locking herself into a rigid meal plan that night. She presented now hoping for some way to feel safe without having to live as though every kindness concealed a threat, though what frightened her most was that she might never fully trust another person’s reassurance, or her own body, enough to let herself be close again.
